newsitem.title: FRANCE: Support mounts in France for civil disobedience call.
newsitem.headline: Support mounts in France for civil disobedience call.

text.p: French intellectuals, painters, doctors and psychiatrists flocked on Friday to back a film-makers' appeal for civil disobedience on a hardline government immigration bill.

The widening movement reflects concern that the government copied the far-right, anti-immigration National Front in drafting the bill. It has snowballed in just a few days since the Front took a fourth southern town in a municipal election.
Writers, theatre directors and actors signed the appeal on Thursday and were joined by academics, journalists, lawyers, painters, and sculptors among others on Friday.

"We call upon our fellow citizens to disobey and not submit to these inhuman laws," the film directors said in their statement, one of several recent protests against a four-year-old government crackdown on illegal immigrants.
"We are guilty, every one of us, of putting up illegal foreign residents recently...We request being probed and put on trial," they added.

Daniel Buren, famed for his controversial striped columns outside Paris's Palais Royal, and other artists pledged to defy plans to require French citizens to report the arrival and departure of foreigners staying at their homes.
They dismissed the centre-right government's bill as "informing on others and inspired by xenophobia".
Some 50 artists and cartoonists will publish drawings against the bill in the left-leaning daily Liberation on Monday.

Jean-Louis Motchane, a physics professor at Paris VII university, said petitions were circulating at the state-run CNRS research agency and other bodies. Fifty-eight physics experts signed a petition on the Internet.
Seven hundred psychoanalysts and a hundred or so lawyers followed suit, signing appeals similar to that launched by the film directors.

"Enough excessive simplifications and dangerous generalisations!" retorted the Gaullist RPR, senior partner in the ruling coalition. "All local politicians know that residence certificates are behind much of the illegal immigration France suffers from," it said in a statement.
Some 150 writers, including Bernard-Henri Levy, Jean Lacouture, and best-selling Marie Darrieussecq, had earlier joined the filmmakers' appeal.
Many of the film directors had demonstrated in the southern port city of Toulon on Thursday against a drive by its National Front mayor to sack the director of a local theatre and close it down.

Former Defence Minister Francois Leotard, a member of the centre-right UDF, junior partner in the ruling coalition, offered to have the Chateauvallon theatre and cultural centre move to Frejus, where he is mayor.
Leotard told TF1 television that intellectuals and artists were "legitimately concerned at the (mayor's) determination to stifle a cultural centre".

In Vitrolles, the depressed southern town which the National Front took in municipal elections on Sunday, police arrested two men after petrol bomb attacks overnight on the town hall and the National Front offices.
No one was hurt but a fire was started at the Front's offices.
The attacks were the latest in a series of violent incidents which began on Sunday when Catherine Megret, the wife of the Front's number two Bruno Megret, won the election run-off.
The poll drew wide attention in France and abroad as commentators said it showed growing support for the party which wants to expel millions of foreigners from France.
Vitrolles is the fourth French town controlled by the Front after it won Toulon, Orange and Marignane in 1995.
